text: Recon gave you an attack surface map built mostly from guesses — domains, IP ranges, technology hints. Scanning is where you finally send real packets at the target and get ground truth back. Nmap, short for Network Mapper, is the tool nearly every pentest report's scanning phase runs through, and this lesson is about actually understanding what each scan type does, not just which flag to type from a cheat sheet.

Nmap reports one of three states per port, and conflating them is the most common beginner mistake. A SYN/ACK coming back means the port is open, and Nmap immediately sends a RST rather than finishing the handshake. A bare RST means closed — nothing is listening. But no response at all, or an ICMP unreachable, means filtered: a firewall most likely dropped the probe, and the question of whether something's really there simply wasn't answered.

That half-open behavior is exactly what the default TCP SYN scan, -sS, is doing when you run it with root or Administrator privileges. nmap -sS against a target host sends a SYN to each port and reads the reply, never completing a full connection. The sample output here shows a typical result — SSH, HTTP, and HTTPS open, and port 3389 filtered, meaning something is blocking that probe rather than confirming the port is closed.

When raw-socket privileges aren't available, -sT falls back to a full TCP connect scan through the OS socket API — slower and more visible in target logs, but it works without elevated access. UDP scanning with -sU is different: there's no handshake, so an unanswered port comes back open or filtered rather than a clean answer, which is why you budget real time and scope it to the top ports rather than all 65,535.

Nmap's six timing templates, -T0 through -T5, aren't a performance setting — they're a rules-of-engagement decision. A paranoid -T0 or -T1 scan can take hours, but it's far less likely to trip an IDS alerting threshold or stress a fragile production host. -T4 or -T5 finish in minutes but generate a traffic burst that's trivial to detect. The right choice depends on what your signed scope actually permits against that specific target.

You now have real, authorized ground truth about which ports are open, closed, or filtered, and a sense of how aggressively you're allowed to ask. Next lesson pushes past the port state itself: -sV version detection, banner grabbing, and how an exact software version — not just an open port — is what actually points toward a known-vulnerable configuration worth investigating further.
